Text and cancellation
Fragment size

Smaller fragments bound unwanted synthesis sooner but add calls and boundary pauses. Larger fragments preserve context but can delay the next item. With whole words this is a target, not a strict maximum: long words remain intact.

Cut boundaries

Allow cuts inside words

Whole words preserve pronunciation. Inside-word cuts bound fragments more tightly but may split words, SSML, URLs, emoji sequences, dictionary matches or verification codes. This is character slicing, not linguistic syllable detection. Unheard audio is discarded on interruption; the remainder stays available while speech continues.
Prepare by fragments above

0 prepares every request by fragments: less work before the first audio, but less context for text rules. Higher values prepare shorter requests in full and may delay their start. Inside-word cuts always use fragment preparation. Experimental scheduling publishes the first transformed piece without transforming the next first.
Prepared queue depth

More prepared fragments may avoid gaps if text processing is slow; they use more memory and waste more work after a swipe. This queues text, not extra audible speech. One fragment minimizes speculative work but may leave the engine waiting.
Text preparation workers

One worker uses less CPU. Two or three allow the next request to prepare while cancelled text work exits. They do not synthesize audio in parallel or make a single transform parallel. Extra workers may increase CPU, battery use and contention. Cancellation is checked between text stages; an individual stage may still take time to finish.
Audio delivery
Audio lead

Less audio ahead of wall time may make interruptions cleaner but may starve playback and cause gaps. More lead tolerates scheduling delays but queues more unheard audio. The limit is checked after each delivered block and can be exceeded by a block; it is not an end-to-end latency guarantee. On automatic playback, the client and Android control discarding audio already delivered.
Native block size
%1$d samples: %2$.1f ms of audio, about %3$.1f callbacks per second of audio

Smaller blocks expose audio and cancellation more often but add copies, locks and wakeups. Larger blocks reduce overhead but make delivery coarser. Aborting delivery still leaves the engine finishing the current text fragment. These figures use the selected output rate; generating a block may be much faster than playing it.
Maximum delivery block
Automatic, framework buffer

Limits how much queued mono audio is read and delivered before checking the lead again. Smaller values bound overshoot but add JNI calls and copies. Larger values reduce overhead but may deliver several native blocks at once. The framework can impose a smaller size; partial blocks have fewer samples. A small delivery block cannot bypass waiting for the native block to be generated.
Native queue capacity

A smaller queue limits synthesis running ahead and discarded work; it can block the producer more often. A larger queue tolerates scheduling delays but permits more speculative audio. This changes active capacity; allocated storage remains reserved for safe reuse.
Capacity: %1$.1f ms of mono PCM at %2$d Hz. This is storage capacity, not a mandatory wait.
Light output processing

Keeps the DC filter and equalizer, skips peak analysis and automatic gain, and replaces the soft limiter with hard clipping. It may reduce CPU cost; volume can change and boosted peaks may sound distorted. Disabled uses the normal processing chain.
App playback only

The next two controls affect app playback on accessibility, media or both routes. Automatic playback belongs to Android and ignores them. The device can impose a larger buffer. This screen does not change your audio route.
Requested playback buffer

Smaller buffers may start sooner but underrun on a busy device. Larger buffers tolerate delays but can increase queued sound. The effective size is at least the device minimum and is aligned to stereo frames.
Playback start threshold

Percentage of the effective playback buffer required to start. Lower values may start sooner but produce gaps; higher values wait for more audio. Available on Android 12 and later. Earlier Android versions use the system threshold. This is not a percentage of total voice latency.
Device trials

These buttons use this installed TTS service, including the experimental path. The interruption trial flushes six items every 350 ms; it simulates new requests, not real TalkBack gestures. Also try navigating with TalkBack and compare the same text, voice, route and sample rate after resetting.
